body: The indicator goes on about two hundred yards early, the way it always does, and the little green arrow ticks on the dashboard. Thursday evening, ten past six, the road he drives every Thursday evening. The turning comes up. He does not take it. The indicator carries on ticking for another quarter of a mile before he notices and cancels it. There is a roundabout further on and he goes round it once, and then, for no reason he could explain to anybody, he goes round it a second time. Then he takes the exit for home and drives back with the radio off.

There is no feeling anywhere in that. He was not weeping and he was not resolved. Something in it was purely geometric: a man was going one way and then he was going another way. That is the whole of what the word means, and almost none of what the word has come to mean.

Repentance has been quietly redefined as remorse. Under that reading a person repents by feeling sufficiently bad about a thing, and the sincerity of the feeling becomes the measure — which is unfortunate, because feeling is the one part of the transaction that nobody else can verify and anybody can generate.

The word does not mean that in either of the languages the text uses. The Hebrew is a word about turning: turning round, turning back, physically going the other way, and it is used of roads and armies and people who have walked off in the wrong direction. The Greek is a word about a change of mind, but in the practical sense — the mind that governs what a person does next week. Both are directional. Both describe somebody who was heading one way and is now heading another, and neither says a single thing about how the person felt while turning. Look for the emotional content in the vocabulary and it is simply not there. What is there is a route.

This band is arranged on the same logic, as it happens. The dial runs from 300.30 to 398.70 in five blocks of twenty whole numbers, and a station is placed by the direction it is aimed rather than by how it makes anybody feel. 46 of the 121 frequencies are on air.

That is a more expensive way to programme than it sounds, because the cheap way to build a Christian station is to build a mood. Pick a feeling — calm, or uplift, or conviction — and select everything that produces it, and you have a coherent-sounding channel within a week. What you do not have is anything that survives the listener no longer feeling it. A station built on direction keeps playing the same material on the days it does nothing for a person at all, which is the test a mood station cannot pass and the week the material is doing its actual work.

The redefinition was not an accident, and it is not confined to religion. Ours is a culture that has made sincerity the highest available proof. An apology is judged by whether it seemed heartfelt. A position is defended by how strongly it is held. Somebody who feels dreadful about a wrong is treated as having partly discharged it, and somebody who has quietly stopped doing the wrong without seeming sorry enough is treated with suspicion. It is a strange arrangement, because it rewards the one thing that costs nothing and cannot be audited.

The result is a spiritual life measured in the wrong units. A person keeps track of how moved they were, how the meeting went, whether they wept, whether the sense of it lasted into Monday. None of that is a route. A route is duller and far more legible: what time you got up, what you did with the money, which conversation you finally had, which road you did not turn down on Thursday. Other people can see a route, including the people you have wronged, who are not remotely interested in your interior weather.
Which brings us to the part that makes this worth an article rather than a footnote in a lexicon.

The case for remorse is real and should be put fairly. Scripture does not treat sorrow as irrelevant; there is such a thing as a godly grief, and the psalms are full of people in genuine anguish about what they have done. A person who wrongs somebody and feels nothing is in a worse condition, not a better one. So the feeling is not the enemy. The trouble is what it is asked to do. Sorrow that changes the route is the beginning of repentance. Sorrow that does not change the route is weather: it arrives, it is genuinely unpleasant, it passes, and the man is standing exactly where he stood before it started.
You can feel terrible for thirty years and never once turn around. Many people have, and they think it counts.

A woman parks in the same car park at ten to seven on a Tuesday, as she has done for three years and two months. She buys the same coffee from the same machine in the foyer, because the good machine is on the floor above and she has never been up there. She sits in the same chair, third from the door, and afterwards she drives home and puts the television on. She feels nothing about any of it. There was a period, early on, when the whole thing was enormous and frightening and she cried in the car most weeks, and that period ended a long time ago and she does not miss it. What is left is a Tuesday, a car park, and a coffee out of the wrong machine. She has not had a drink in three years and two months.
The emotion left and the direction stayed, and the direction is the thing that saved her. That is the mechanism, and it is the exact inverse of what the redefinition promises.

It is only honest to say that this makes repentance sound mechanical and a bit joyless, and to some extent it is. It removes a comfort a great many sincere people are relying on. If feeling bad is not the payment, thirty years of feeling bad has bought nothing, and that is a bleak thing to be told at sixty. It also leaves nowhere to hide, because a route can be checked and a feeling cannot.

But the alternative is worse, and it is worth naming what it does to somebody. Remorse is comfortable in one very specific way: it feels like the cost has been paid. A man who is miserable about a thing experiences his own misery as evidence of a tender conscience, and the misery becomes proof that he is not the sort of person who does that — while he continues to do it. That is not a hard heart. It is more efficient than a hard heart, because it runs on real sorrow and produces no change at all. The bleakness of the directional reading is the bleakness of an honest instrument.

So the question is never how sorry you are. It is which way you are now walking, and that is not answered by introspection at all. It is answered by a diary, a bank statement, a route, a Thursday. Repentance is a turn. It can come with tears or with nothing much. It can happen on an evening when a man is not consciously thinking about God and simply does not take a turning he has taken every week for years. What makes it repentance is not the temperature. It is the heading.
All of which is theory until something is actually playing. So here is the part that is not theory.

Turning is not a genre and there is no station on this dial called Repentance, which is probably just as well. What there is instead is a band arranged by direction, and one stretch of it that is unusually good for the purpose here. The Nations block, HM 320 to HM 340, carries worship hosted in its own language rather than translated into it afterwards, station by station, across 29 languages. Most of it will be in a language you do not speak. That would be a defect on a mood station. On a directional one it is close to an advantage, for a reason that takes one more paragraph to explain.

Put HM 323.10 Deutschland Inspire on. Two reasons, and the second is the real one. The first is that German keeps this article’s meaning out in the open: its ordinary word for repentance is Umkehr, which is not a word about sorrow at all but about turning round, an about-face, the thing you do at a roundabout. A language that cannot say the word without saying the direction is a useful corrective for an English ear. The second reason is that you will not follow the lyrics. Every emotional handle is removed. What is left is the bare practice of having put it on, and having put it on again the next morning, which is exactly the unit repentance is measured in. Nobody was ever argued into turning round. They found themselves further along a different road.

There is nothing to install. No app, no download, no card. Open kJubilee.com on whatever phone or laptop is nearest, press play, and it plays — the site is built for inexpensive devices and thin connections, so it starts on the hardware people actually have. Add the page to your home screen if you would like it nearer to hand. And do make yourself an account while you are there. It is free, it keeps your favourites with you across every Jubilee site, and it is how this band learns which frequencies people are genuinely reaching for, which is how the next one gets built.

So take this as an invitation rather than a rebuke. Do not go away and work on feeling worse; that is the whole error this article is about, and you are probably good at it already. Put HM 323.10 on tomorrow morning while you are doing something ordinary, and then again the morning after, and notice that on the second morning you felt nothing much and did it anyway. That is the shape of the thing. Not a mood that arrives. A heading you hold when the mood has gone.
